d: A vehicle electronics layout in which zone ECUs placed in each area of the car connect nearby sensors and actuators, while control processing is concentrated in a central high-performance computer. It allows a shorter, lighter wiring harness than the traditional one-ECU-per-function approach.

k: SOTIF(意図した機能の安全性)

n.ja: SOTIF(意図した機能の安全性)

d: The concept that addresses hazards arising without any component failure, from sensor performance limits, insufficient specifications or reasonably foreseeable misuse. It is standardized as ISO 21448 and is central to developing automated driving and driver-assistance systems.

k: シリコンフォトニクス

n.ja: シリコンフォトニクス

d: Technology for integrating optical circuits such as waveguides, modulators and photodetectors on silicon. It uses the materials and processes of CMOS fabs, enabling volume production on 200 mm or 300 mm wafers. Because silicon emits light poorly, lasers are added using compound semiconductors.

A structure that confines and guides light by surrounding a high-index core with a lower-index cladding. Silicon photonics commonly uses silicon about 0.5 µm × 0.22 µm in cross section surrounded by oxide, allowing bend radii of just a few µm.

The speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in a material. At a wavelength of 1.55 µm, silicon is about 3.48 and oxide (SiO2) about 1.45; the larger this contrast, the more tightly light can be confined in a small waveguide.

The optical fiber communication band around 1530 to 1565 nm. Silica fiber loss is lowest there (about 0.2 dB/km) and erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) can amplify it, so it is used for long-haul links and dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM).

The optical fiber communication band around 1260 to 1360 nm. It includes the region near 1.31 µm where chromatic dispersion in standard single-mode fiber is nearly zero, and is widely used for short links such as those inside data centers.

The fraction of optical power lost to scattering and absorption as light travels through a waveguide or fiber, expressed in dB/cm or dB/km. In silicon waveguides the main cause is scattering from sidewall roughness, with typical values around 1 to 3 dB/cm, far higher than fiber's roughly 0.2 dB/km.

k: グレーティングカプラ

n.ja: グレーティングカプラ

d: A device that etches a periodic grating into a waveguide so that diffraction redirects light to couple with an optical fiber positioned above the chip. Its advantage is that optical testing is possible on the wafer before dicing, but its coupling bandwidth is narrow and it is polarization dependent.

A device that couples light by butting an optical fiber against the edge facet of the chip. An inverse taper that narrows the waveguide tip expands the optical mode to match the fiber. It offers low loss over a wide wavelength range but needs facet preparation and is hard to test at wafer level.

k: シングルモードファイバ

n.ja: シングルモードファイバ

d: Optical fiber that carries only one propagation mode, with a core diameter of about 9 µm. With no pulse spreading from different modes traveling at different speeds (modal dispersion), it is used for long-distance and high-speed links.

k: マッハツェンダー変調器

n.ja: マッハツェンダー変調器

d: A modulator that splits incoming light into two arms, shifts the phase between them by changing the arms' refractive index with an electrical signal, and recombines them to turn the phase change into an intensity change. A phase difference of 0 gives maximum brightness and π gives minimum. Silicon versions use the plasma dispersion effect and are a few mm long.

k: キャリア分散効果(プラズマ分散効果)

n.ja: キャリア分散効果(プラズマ分散効果)
n.zh-hant: 載子色散效應(電漿色散效應)

d: The change in refractive index and optical absorption of a semiconductor when its free electron or hole concentration changes. Because silicon has almost no Pockels effect, this effect is used to shift phase in silicon modulators. Increasing the carrier concentration lowers the refractive index.

A looped waveguide that resonates only at wavelengths for which one round trip's optical length is an integer number of wavelengths. It is used as a wavelength filter or compact modulator. In silicon the resonance shifts by about 0.08 nm per °C, so heaters are often used to control its temperature.

A method of carrying separate signals on different wavelengths of light and sending them together over a single fiber. CWDM uses wide 20 nm spacing, while DWDM packs many wavelengths at narrow spacings such as 100 GHz (about 0.8 nm).

In intensity modulation, the ratio of the optical power P1 for a "1" to the power P0 for a "0", expressed in dB as 10 log(P1/P0). The larger it is, the greater the difference between 1 and 0 and the fewer decision errors at the receiver.

k: CPO(コパッケージドオプティクス)

n.ja: CPO(コパッケージドオプティクス)

d: Technology that mounts the optical transceiver parts (optical engines) in the same package as a switch IC or similar. Shorter electrical connections lower the energy per bit, but the optics cannot be swapped out by unplugging, so testing before assembly and the use of external laser sources become important.

The broadening of light pulses in an optical fiber because light of different wavelengths travels at slightly different speeds. In standard single-mode fiber it is nearly zero near 1.31 µm and about 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1.55 µm.

A Japanese semiconductor manufacturer founded in 2022 to mass-produce leading-edge logic chips at the 2 nm generation. It has a fab in Chitose, Hokkaido, and plans to start volume production in 2027 as a foundry that manufactures chips designed by other companies.
Volatile memory that stores each bit in a cell of one transistor and one capacitor and needs periodic refresh before the charge leaks away. It is used as main memory in PCs and servers.

A reliability test that operates products at high temperature under voltage for a long time to accelerate and evaluate chip lifetime and failure rate. A typical condition is 1000 hours at around 125 °C.

k: 高温高湿バイアス試験(THB)

n.ja: 高温高湿バイアス試験(THB)

d: A reliability test that applies voltage in a hot, humid environment, typically 85 °C/85% RH, to evaluate corrosion and increased leakage caused by moisture entering the package. It is also called the 85/85 test.

k: 高温放置試験(高温保存試験)

n.ja: 高温放置試験(高温保存試験)

d: A reliability test that keeps products at high temperature without applying voltage to evaluate degradation of wire-bond joints, data retention in nonvolatile memory and similar effects. It is also called HTS or HTSL.

A reliability test that repeatedly applies high and low temperatures to evaluate solder-joint fatigue and package cracking or delamination caused by differences in thermal expansion between materials.

A surface-mount package with terminals exposed around the perimeter of its underside and no leads projecting from the sides. The central thermal pad on the bottom can be soldered to the board, making it small with good heat dissipation.
A surface-mount package with gull-wing leads extending from all four sides. Its joints are easy to inspect visually, and it is widely used for microcontrollers and similar ICs.
A storage device that stores data using NAND flash memory and a controller. It has no moving parts and offers faster random access and better shock resistance than an HDD.

A field-effect transistor whose gate is a pn junction, controlling channel current through the width of the depletion layer that grows under reverse bias. Most are depletion-mode devices that conduct at a gate voltage of 0 V.
Light in the deep-ultraviolet range used in semiconductor lithography. DUV lithography generally refers to exposure using KrF excimer lasers (248 nm) and ArF excimer lasers (193 nm) as light sources.

The collective term for the equipment that automatically moves wafer carriers such as FOUPs between tools and storage in a semiconductor fab, and the control system that runs it. It consists of OHTs, stockers and related equipment.

A package substrate whose core is a sheet of glass instead of glass-fiber-reinforced resin. Because glass is flat and dimensionally stable, it is being developed to form fine wiring and dense through-vias even in large packages.

k: パネルレベルパッケージ(PLP)

n.ja: パネルレベルパッケージ(PLP)

d: A method that manufactures many packages at once on a large rectangular panel instead of a round wafer. It uses area efficiently and can lower cost, but warpage, die shift over large areas and equipment standardization are challenges.

DRAM that stacks memory cells vertically in many layers to increase capacity without relying only on planar shrinking. Handling the capacitor is the biggest challenge, and as of the mid-2020s it is still in research and development.

Layered materials that remain stable at a thickness of one to a few atomic layers. Semiconductors such as MoS2 can form extremely thin channels that are difficult with silicon, so they are being researched for future ultra-scaled transistors.

Three-dimensional integration in which transistor layers are built one after another on a single wafer. Layers can be connected far more finely than by bonding finished chips, but the upper layers must be made at low temperature. Also called sequential 3D integration.

Technologies and the approach of integrating optical and electronic circuits very close together or as one unit, replacing electrical wiring with light. The aim is to cut power by extending optical links from between equipment to between boards and between chips. The Japanese term (kōden yūgō) is widely used in Japan.

A semiconductor made from diamond, a crystal of carbon. With a bandgap of about 5.5 eV, one of the highest thermal conductivities of any material and a high breakdown field, it is promising for high-voltage, high-frequency and high-temperature devices, but n-type doping and large substrates are difficult.

k: ニューロモーフィックコンピューティング

n.ja: ニューロモーフィックコンピューティング

d: Computing that imitates neurons and synapses in the brain, exchanging information as pulses called spikes and computing only when something changes. It places memory close to computation and aims for low power.

A technique that uses the tendency of block copolymers to form regular fine patterns on their own, aligning their position and orientation with guides made by lithography to create patterns finer than the resolution limit. Reducing defects to extremely low levels is the challenge for volume production.

An error-detection method that treats the data bits as a polynomial, appends the remainder of dividing it by a generator polynomial, and lets the receiver repeat the calculation to detect errors. It is widely used in Ethernet, PCI Express, USB and file formats.

A model that organizes communication functions into seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. It serves as a common vocabulary for thinking about each layer's role separately.
A 32-bit value that shows how many upper bits of an IP address represent the network (the network part). Written like 255.255.255.0, which means the same as /24 in CIDR notation.
A system, managed in a distributed way by servers around the world, that maps domain names such as www.example.com to the IP addresses used for communication.

A technique that rewrites the IP addresses of packets passing through a router. The variant that also rewrites port numbers so many devices can share one global address is called NAPT (IP masquerading).
The procedure that establishes a TCP connection. Three exchanges, the client's SYN, the server's SYN+ACK and the client's ACK, confirm each side's initial sequence number.
The 48-bit address used in Ethernet and wireless LAN to identify devices within the same network. The upper 24 bits identify the manufacturer, and it is assigned to each interface at manufacture.
Address Resolution Protocol. A protocol that finds the MAC address of a device on the same network from its IP address. The request is broadcast, and the matching device replies.

k: デフォルトゲートウェイ

n.ja: デフォルトゲートウェイ

d: The router to which a host hands packets for destinations on other networks. The host uses its subnet mask to decide whether a destination is on the same network, and sends to this router if not.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. A protocol that automatically assigns devices joining a network an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers and other settings for a limited time.
Transport Layer Security. A protocol that encrypts communication, detects tampering and authenticates servers with certificates. HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS.

The access control method used in wireless LAN. A station checks that the channel is idle, waits an additional random time before sending, and confirms delivery with an ACK from the receiver, so as to avoid collisions as far as possible.

Virtual LAN. A function that creates logically separate networks (broadcast domains) on the same physical equipment, typically per switch port. Between switches, VLANs are distinguished by IEEE 802.1Q tags.
A number from 0 to 65535 used by TCP and UDP to identify which application on a host the traffic is for. Ports 0–1023, such as 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS and 53 for DNS, are called well-known ports.

Classless Inter-Domain Routing. The scheme of freely setting the length of the network part of an IP address as a number of bits (the prefix length) after a slash, as in 192.168.1.0/24, and that notation.

A cryptographic method that uses a matched pair of different keys for encryption and decryption: a public key and a private key. The public key may be known to anyone, while only its owner holds the private key. It makes key distribution easy but is computationally heavy, so it is combined with symmetric-key cryptography for encrypting the data itself. RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography are typical examples.

A function that computes a value of fixed length (a hash value) from data of any length. Those used in cryptography, such as SHA-256, are built so that it is practically impossible either to find the original data from a hash value or to find two pieces of data with the same hash value, and they are used for detecting tampering, digital signatures and password storage.

A technique for confirming who created an electronic document and that it has not been altered since. The signer processes the document's hash value with their own private key to create the signature, and the recipient verifies it with the signer's public key. It is also used for non-repudiation.

Authentication that verifies a person by combining two or more different factors among knowledge (such as a password), possession (such as a smartphone or smart card) and inherence (such as a fingerprint or face). Even if the password leaks, logging in is impossible without the other factors. Also called MFA.

An attack that exploits a web application building SQL statements by simply concatenating user input, using the input to change the meaning of the command and manipulate the database without authorization. Prepared statements with placeholders are the fundamental countermeasure.

A cryptographic method that uses the same key for encryption and decryption, also called secret-key cryptography. Its computation is light and it can encrypt large amounts of data quickly, but securely sharing the key with the other party (key distribution) is a challenge. AES is a typical example.

k: メッセージ認証コード

n.ja: メッセージ認証コード

d: A short value (MAC) computed from a message and a symmetric key shared by the sender and receiver. By recomputing it with the same key and comparing, the receiver can confirm that the message came from someone who knows the key and was not altered. Because the receiver can also create the same value, it cannot provide non-repudiation. HMAC is a typical example.

The idea of giving users, programs and services only the minimum privileges needed to do their job. It keeps the scope of damage small even if an account is taken over, malware runs or someone makes a mistake.

k: クロスサイトスクリプティング(XSS)

n.ja: クロスサイトスクリプティング(XSS)

d: A vulnerability in which a web application outputs user input into HTML as is, so that a script contained in the input runs in visitors' browsers as a page of that site. Escaping characters with special meaning on output is the fundamental countermeasure.

Malware that makes files on a computer unusable, for example by encrypting them, and demands a ransom in exchange for restoring them. Some attackers also threaten to publish stolen data. Backups kept disconnected from the network are an important safeguard.

A fraud technique that lures people to fake websites through emails, text messages and the like posing as real companies or organizations, and gets them to enter IDs, passwords, credit card numbers and so on, which are then stolen.

A random value added for each user when computing the hash value of a password. It makes the same password produce different hash values, making cracking with tables of precomputed hash values difficult. It is stored together with the hash value and does not need to be kept secret.

An attack that exploits a software vulnerability in the period after it is discovered but before a fix (patch) is provided. Since patches cannot prevent it, damage is limited with multiple layers of defense.

k: ソーシャルエンジニアリング

n.ja: ソーシャルエンジニアリング

d: The general term for techniques that exploit people's psychology, habits and carelessness rather than technical means, to get them to reveal important information such as passwords or to perform actions. Examples include impersonation calls, peeking over someone's shoulder (shoulder surfing) and rummaging through trash (dumpster diving).

A database that represents data as tables (relations) of rows and columns and relates tables to each other through shared values. Also called an RDB. Queries and updates are made in SQL, and constraints such as primary keys and foreign keys keep the data consistent.

The standard language for defining tables, searching, inserting, updating and deleting data, and controlling privileges in relational databases. It is standardized by ISO/IEC. Its statements include SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE TABLE and GRANT.

A column, or set of columns, used to uniquely identify one row in a table. It carries the constraints that its values must not be duplicated and must not include NULL. The primary key is chosen from among the minimal sets of columns that can identify a row uniquely (candidate keys).

A column that refers to the primary key (or a unique column) of another table. Through the referential integrity constraint, which allows only values that exist in the referenced table or NULL, it prevents data that points to nonexistent rows. The behavior when a referenced row is deleted or updated (rejection, cascading deletion and so on) can also be specified.

A design procedure that splits relational database tables based on functional dependencies between columns so that the same fact is not recorded in several places. It removes duplicated data and prevents update, insertion and deletion anomalies. Its stages include first to third normal form and Boyce-Codd normal form.

The state of a table that is in second normal form and has no column determined via a column other than the primary key (no transitive functional dependency). If there is a dependency such as emp_no → dept_code → dept_name, for example, splitting off a department table gives third normal form.

A diagram depicting the things managed in a database (entities) and the relationships between them. Relationships have multiplicities such as one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many. A many-to-many relationship is implemented in tables by adding an associative entity that holds both primary keys as foreign keys, breaking it into two one-to-many relationships.

A series of operations on a database treated as a single unit. COMMIT makes the results permanent, and ROLLBACK returns the data to its state before the transaction began. The DBMS manages transactions with locks and logs so that they satisfy atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability (the ACID properties).

The initials of four properties a transaction should satisfy: atomicity (everything is executed or nothing is), consistency (integrity constraints keep being satisfied), isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other) and durability (committed results are not lost even if a failure occurs).

A setting that determines how far interference between concurrently running transactions is prevented. The SQL standard defines four levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE. Higher levels prevent more of dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom reads, but reduce the amount of work that can be processed concurrently.

A concurrency control method in which each transaction has two phases, one acquiring locks and one releasing them, and acquires no new locks once it starts releasing. It guarantees serializability, but deadlocks can still occur.

A data structure in a database for quickly finding, from a value in a particular column of a table, the location of the rows holding that value. B+ trees are commonly used. It makes searches faster but must be maintained every time a row is inserted, updated or deleted, and it uses storage.

In a relational database, a virtual table defined by giving a name to a SELECT statement. It normally holds no data of its own and builds its result from the underlying tables each time it is referenced. It is used to simplify complex queries and to restrict access by limiting the columns and rows shown.

A collective term for databases other than relational databases, including key-value, document, column-oriented and graph types. Many products are easy to scale out across multiple servers and allow flexible data formats, but they are often poor at complex queries such as table joins and at strict consistency.

A description of how the work (time complexity) or memory (space complexity) an algorithm needs grows with the number of data items n. It is written in Big-O notation, such as O(n), O(n log n) or O(n²), dropping constant factors and lower-order terms.

A sort that keeps elements with equal keys in their original relative order. Bubble sort, insertion sort and merge sort are stable, while selection sort, quicksort and heapsort are generally not. Stability is needed when sorting by several keys in turn.

A data structure that computes a storage position from a key with a hash function, allowing search, insertion and deletion in O(1) on average. Collisions, where different keys map to the same position, are handled by chaining or open addressing.

A search method for sorted data that compares the target with the middle element and halves the search range each time. It finds a value among n items in at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons, so its complexity is O(log n). The data must be sorted.

A binary tree in which, for every node, all values in the left subtree are smaller and all values in the right subtree are larger than the node. Search, insertion and deletion take time proportional to the tree's height, and an in-order traversal visits the values in ascending order.

A complete binary tree in which each parent's value is greater than or equal to (max-heap) or less than or equal to (min-heap) its children's values. It can be stored in an array: with the root at a[0], the children of a[i] are a[2i+1] and a[2i+2]. Reading the maximum (minimum) takes O(1), and insertion and removal take O(log n); it is used for priority queues and heapsort.

A data structure in which each element holds a value and a pointer to the next element, and the elements are linked by following the pointers. Once the position is known, insertion and deletion are O(1) pointer changes, but reading the i-th element requires walking from the front, O(n). The elements tend to be scattered in memory, so caches work less well than with arrays.

A last-in, first-out (LIFO) data structure in which the element added last is removed first. Adding an element is called push and removing one is called pop. Stacks are used to manage return addresses and local variables in function calls (the call stack), to evaluate expressions in Reverse Polish notation and for depth-first search.

A first-in, first-out (FIFO) data structure in which the element added first is removed first. Adding to the back is called enqueue and removing from the front is called dequeue. Queues are used for waiting lines of work, passing data between tasks and breadth-first search.

A function calling itself as part of its own processing. The problem is split into smaller problems of the same form, and the calls stop at a case that is not split further (the base case). Each call uses stack space, so recursion that is too deep overflows the stack. Tail recursion, where the recursive call is the last thing the function does, can be converted into a loop.

An algorithm design method that splits a problem into smaller subproblems and records their answers in a table for reuse, avoiding repeated computation of the same thing. It is used for the knapsack problem, minimum-coin change, the longest common subsequence, shortest paths and more.

An algorithm design method that builds a solution by repeatedly picking the choice that looks best at that moment, without revisiting earlier choices. It is fast and simple, but it gives an optimal solution only when the problem has special properties, as with coin systems like Japan's or Kruskal's algorithm for minimum spanning trees.

A way of searching a graph or tree that visits vertices in order of distance from the start: first those one edge away, then those two edges away, and so on. It is implemented with a queue, and in a graph without edge weights it finds the smallest number of edges from the start to every vertex. It is abbreviated BFS.

A way of searching a graph or tree that goes as far as possible along one path and backtracks to try another path when it reaches a dead end. It is implemented with recursion or a stack and is used for maze solving, finding connected components and cycles, and topological sorting. It is abbreviated DFS.

An algorithm that finds the shortest paths from one starting vertex to every vertex in a graph whose edge weights are 0 or greater. It repeatedly finalizes the nearest vertex whose distance is not yet final and updates the distances of its neighbors. It does not work correctly with negative edge weights.

The unit that represents information in a quantum computer. It can be in a superposition α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ of |0⟩ and |1⟩, and a measurement gives 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|². Qubits are realized with superconducting circuits, ions, neutral atoms, electron spins in silicon, photons and more.

The ability of a quantum system such as a qubit to be in a state formed by adding several states, such as |0⟩ and |1⟩, with complex amplitudes. A measurement gives one of the outcomes at random, and differences in the phases of the amplitudes affect the results through interference.

A link between the states of several qubits that cannot be written as a combination of the states of the individual qubits. In (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, the two measurement results always agree. It is one of the sources of the computing power of quantum computers, but it cannot be used to send information faster than light.

A basic operation that changes the state of qubits. There are single-qubit gates such as X (bit flip), Z (phase flip) and H (Hadamard) and two-qubit gates such as CNOT, and they can be represented as rotations on the Bloch sphere. They are implemented with microwave pulses for superconducting qubits and with lasers and similar means for ions and neutral atoms.

The process by which a qubit, through interactions with its environment, loses the phase and energy information of its superposition and its quantum properties break down. Its speed is described by the energy relaxation time T1 and the dephasing time T2.

A superconducting qubit that combines a Josephson junction with a capacitor. Its frequency is generally a few GHz, and the nonlinearity of the junction makes the energy levels unequally spaced, so the two lowest levels are used as a qubit. Its design makes it insensitive to charge noise, and it is widely used in superconducting platforms.

A structure in which two superconductors are separated by a thin insulating film or similar layer about 1–2 nm thick. A superconducting current flows through it without producing a voltage, and it acts as a lossless nonlinear inductor. It is used in superconducting qubits, ultra-sensitive magnetic sensors (SQUIDs), voltage standards and more. For qubits it is usually made of aluminum and its oxide.

A refrigerator that uses a mixture of helium-3 and helium-4 to produce cryogenic temperatures of about 10 mK continuously. It is used to operate superconducting qubits and silicon spin qubits. The cooling power of its coldest stage is small, roughly ten to several tens of µW, so heat flowing in through the wiring is a challenge for scaling up.

A device that holds ions in a vacuum with electric fields or similar means, or the quantum computing approach that uses one. Electronic energy levels of the ions serve as qubits and are controlled with lasers or microwaves. All the qubits are identical, with long coherence times and high fidelities, but gates are slower than in superconducting platforms.

An approach that uses the spin direction of electrons or atomic nuclei as qubits. In silicon, single electrons are confined in quantum dots formed by gate electrodes. The qubits are small and are expected to be integrated using CMOS fabrication technology. To reduce noise from nuclear spins, silicon enriched in ²⁸Si is used.

A technology that spreads the information of one logical qubit over many physical qubits and measures only clues to the errors (the syndrome), so that errors can be found and corrected during a computation. It must handle both bit-flip and phase-flip errors and requires the physical error rate to be well below a threshold.

A code for quantum error correction in which qubits are arranged on a two-dimensional grid and errors are detected using only operations between neighboring qubits. Its threshold is high, roughly 1%, and it suits superconducting qubit chips well. The rotated version with code distance d uses 2d² − 1 physical qubits per logical qubit.

k: ショアのアルゴリズム

n.ja: ショアのアルゴリズム

d: A quantum algorithm that solves factoring of large integers and the discrete logarithm problem in polynomial time by finding periods with the quantum Fourier transform. It was published by Peter Shor in 1994. It can break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, but running it requires a large fault-tolerant quantum computer.

Cryptography that bases its security on mathematical problems believed to be hard to solve efficiently even for quantum computers, such as lattice problems and hash functions. It runs on conventional computers and is used to replace RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, which Shor's algorithm can break.

Short for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum: intermediate-scale quantum computers with noise (errors) that do not perform full-scale error correction. The term was proposed by John Preskill in 2018. Because the depth of circuit they can run is limited by gate error rates, error mitigation and methods that combine quantum and classical computation are being studied.

k: ウォーターフォールモデル

n.ja: ウォーターフォールモデル

d: A software development model in which phases such as requirements definition, design, programming and testing are carried out in order from upstream, and in principle the next phase starts only after the previous phase's deliverables are finalized. Planning and progress are easy to control, but an error in the requirements found in a later phase causes a lot of rework.

A development model that arranges the phases going down from requirements definition through design to implementation and the testing phases going back up from unit testing to acceptance testing in a V shape, and pairs the two sides, such as requirements definition with acceptance testing, design with integration and system testing, and module design with unit testing. Which design phase is paired with which test differs slightly between organizations and textbooks.

A general term for ways of developing software that repeat short iterations of a few weeks, produce working software each time, incorporate user feedback and revise the plan to follow changing requirements. Representative methods include Scrum and Extreme Programming (XP).

A representative framework of agile development. With three roles, the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and the Developers, and the events held within Sprints of a fixed length of one month or less (Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective), a working product is built a little at a time.

A way of developing software in a short repeated cycle: first write a test for the feature to be built, then write the minimum code to make the test pass, then refactor while keeping the tests passing. It spread as a practice of Extreme Programming (XP).

k: CI/CD(継続的インテグレーション・継続的デリバリー)

n.ja: CI/CD(継続的インテグレーション・継続的デリバリー)

d: A combined name for continuous integration (CI), in which developers merge their changes into a shared branch frequently and each merge triggers a build and automated tests, and continuous delivery (CD), which keeps tested changes ready to be released to production at any time. When the release itself is also automated, it is called continuous deployment.

k: ブラックボックステスト

n.ja: ブラックボックステスト

d: A testing approach that determines inputs and expected outputs from the specification alone, without looking at the internal structure of the program. Its techniques include equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis and decision tables.

k: ホワイトボックステスト

n.ja: ホワイトボックステスト

d: A testing approach that creates test cases based on the internal structure of a program (statements, branches and conditions) and checks how much of it has been executed using coverage criteria such as statement coverage and branch coverage. It is used mainly in unit testing.

A black-box testing technique that divides the inputs into groups that the program should handle in the same way (equivalence classes) and tests one representative value from each class. Both valid classes of accepted inputs and invalid classes of inputs that should cause an error are chosen.

A black-box testing technique that, because defects tend to cluster at the boundaries between equivalence classes, tests the values immediately on both sides of each boundary (for example 0, 1, 100 and 101 when 1 to 100 is accepted). It is good at finding errors such as confused comparison operators.

A white-box testing coverage criterion that requires both the true and false branches of every decision (such as an if statement) in a program to be executed at least once. It is also called decision coverage or C1, and it is stronger than statement coverage (C0), which requires every statement to be executed at least once.

A tree that breaks down the deliverables of a project and the work needed for them from the top level to lower levels. The lowest elements are called work packages and are the units for estimating, scheduling, assigning people and tracking progress.

A scheduling technique that uses the durations of a project's activities and the order relations between them to find each activity's earliest and latest start and its float, and then finds the longest path connecting activities with zero float (the critical path) and the total project duration. A delay in any activity on the critical path delays the whole project.

k: アーンドバリューマネジメント(EVM)

n.ja: アーンドバリューマネジメント(EVM)

d: A technique for managing a project's progress and cost by comparing them on a monetary scale using the planned value (PV), earned value (EV) and actual cost (AC). The schedule performance index SPI = EV ÷ PV and the cost performance index CPI = EV ÷ AC are used to judge delays and budget overruns and to estimate the total cost at completion.

An agreement between the provider and the user of an IT service that sets the quality levels, such as availability, response time, time to recover from failures and support hours, together with how they are measured and what happens if they are not met.

A way of writing an algorithm's steps that does not depend on any particular programming language. Part B of Japan's Fundamental Information Technology Engineer Examination presents programs in a pseudo-language that defines type declarations, assignment with ←, control structures such as if, while and for, and array indices that start at 1.

A table that records how the values of variables change as a program is executed line by line by hand. It is used to check the number of iterations and the final values and to locate mistakes. Because it is done on paper, it is also called desk checking.
A named container that holds a value in a program. It is declared with a type such as integer or real and changed by assignment. Assigning a new value discards the previous one.

A data structure that stores values of the same type in sequence and identifies each element by an index. Because the elements are stored contiguously in memory, the position of any element can be computed from its index, so any element can be read or written in constant time. Some languages start indices at 0, while some notations start them at 1.

A basic structure that determines the flow of a program. There are three: sequence, which runs statements in order from the top; selection (conditional branching), which chooses statements according to a condition; and iteration, which repeats statements, for example while a condition holds. Any procedure is known to be expressible as a combination of these three (the structured program theorem).

A value passed when calling a function or procedure. The variable that receives the value in the declaration is called a formal parameter, and the value passed at the call is called an actual argument. Arguments can be passed by value, which copies the value, or by reference, which lets the callee refer to the variable or array itself.
The value a function returns to its caller when it finishes. In pseudocode, the value of the expression written after return becomes the return value, and the function ends when return is executed.

A way of evaluating the logical operators and and or that skips the right side when the left side alone decides the result. With and, the right side is not evaluated if the left side is false; with or, if the left side is true. It is often used to prevent out-of-range accesses by putting the array range check on the left.

A mistake in which a loop count or an array range is off by exactly one. It arises from whether the final value is included, whether indices start at 0 or 1, and confusing the number of intervals with the number of points (the fence-post problem). Tracing with the boundary values makes it easier to find.

Division of integers that produces an integer quotient. How the fractional part is handled differs between languages: some truncate toward zero (C, Java), and others round down toward negative infinity (Python's //). The results are the same for positive numbers but differ for negative ones.

An operation that gives the remainder of a division, written mod in the pseudo-language and % in many languages. x mod 10 gives the ones digit, x mod 2 tells whether x is even or odd, and i mod n + 1 gives an index that cycles through 1 to n. The sign of the remainder for negative numbers differs between languages.

An operation that treats an integer as a sequence of binary bits and applies AND, OR, exclusive OR (XOR) or NOT to each bit, or shifts the bits left or right. It is used to extract or set particular bits, to count 1 bits, and to multiply or divide by powers of 2.

An approach that builds programs from objects, each bundling data with the procedures (methods) that operate on it. The blueprint for objects is called a class, each object created from a class is called an instance, and each instance has its own values of the member variables.

The error that arises when a real number is represented with a finite number of digits and a value that cannot be represented is rounded to a nearby one. 0.1 cannot be represented exactly as a binary floating-point number, so errors build up when it is added repeatedly, and adding 0.1 ten times in double precision does not give 1.0. Avoid comparing real numbers with = and counting loop iterations with real numbers.
The sales or sales volume at which sales exactly equal costs (the sum of variable and fixed costs), so profit is zero. Break-even sales are found as fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio.

A cost that rises and falls in proportion to production volume or sales, such as material costs, outsourcing costs and sales commissions. The ratio of variable costs to sales is called the variable cost ratio.
A cost incurred in a constant amount each period regardless of production volume or sales, such as depreciation of equipment and buildings, rent and the salaries of permanent employees.
Sales minus variable costs: the amount that covers fixed costs and produces profit. Its ratio to sales is the contribution margin ratio, equal to 1 − variable cost ratio.

The accounting procedure of allocating the acquisition cost of long-lived assets such as equipment and buildings as an expense over the period of use (the useful life). Typical methods are the straight-line and declining-balance methods.

Net income divided by equity: how much profit a company earned relative to the funds provided by shareholders. It equals ROA (return on assets) multiplied by financial leverage (total assets ÷ equity).
A method of working out strategy by sorting internal factors of the company into strengths and weaknesses, and external factors of the environment into opportunities and threats.

k: プロダクトポートフォリオマネジメント(PPM)

n.ja: プロダクトポートフォリオマネジメント(PPM)

d: A method of classifying businesses or products into four groups (stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs) along two axes, market growth rate and relative market share, to decide how to allocate management resources. It was proposed by Boston Consulting Group.

k: ファイブフォース分析

n.ja: ファイブフォース分析

d: A method, proposed by Michael Porter, of analyzing an industry's profitability through five competitive forces: rivalry among existing competitors, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitutes, the bargaining power of suppliers and the bargaining power of buyers.

A framework, proposed by Michael Porter, that divides a company's activities into primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) and support activities, to analyze which activities create value and where costs arise.

k: プロダクトライフサイクル

n.ja: プロダクトライフサイクル

d: A model that divides the period from a product's launch to its disappearance from the market into four stages (introduction, growth, maturity and decline) to consider how sales and profit change and which strategies suit each stage.

A method that sorts items in descending order of sales or usage value, divides them into groups A, B and C by cumulative share, and manages them differently according to their importance. It is done using a Pareto chart.

The sum of the future cash flows from an investment converted to present value using a discount rate, minus the amount invested. If it is greater than zero, the investment is judged worthwhile at that discount rate.

A financial statement that compares revenues and expenses over a period (the accounting period) to show a company's operating results. Subtracting expenses from sales step by step, it shows gross profit, operating profit, ordinary profit (in Japanese statements), profit before income taxes and net income.

A right that protects a technical idea (an invention). It arises when an application is filed with the patent office, examined and registered, and in principle gives the exclusive right to work the invention for 20 years from filing. In exchange, the content of the invention is published.

A redundancy scheme in which two systems perform the same processing at the same time and operate while comparing the results. Errors can be noticed from disagreements in the results, and if one system fails the other continues processing as is. Reliability is high, but the cost is large because two sets of equipment do the same work.

k: デュプレックスシステム

n.ja: デュプレックスシステム

d: A redundancy scheme that builds a system from a primary (active) system that does the processing and a standby system kept ready for failures, and switches to the standby to continue processing when the primary fails. Depending on how ready the standby is, it is classified as hot standby, warm standby or cold standby.

A scheme in a duplex system in which the standby system is kept running and the primary's data is always reflected to it. When the primary fails, processing can switch to the standby and continue in a short time. A scheme that keeps the standby stopped and starts it after a failure is called a cold standby.

A point where a stop in just that one place stops the whole system. Besides equipment that is not made redundant, a shared power supply, a network line or a configuration file can also be a single point of failure. In reliability design, finding single points of failure and making them redundant is a basic step.

A device or software that distributes users' requests among several servers to spread the load. It checks the state of each server regularly (health checks) and removes failed servers from distribution, so it also serves a redundancy role. Unless it is itself made redundant, the load balancer becomes a single point of failure.

A way of raising the processing capacity of a whole system by adding servers and sharing the processing among them. Compared with scale-up, which makes the parts of one server faster, capacity is easier to add and redundancy is gained, but the system must be designed so that the processing can be divided. Reducing the number of servers is called scale-in.

The design concept of making a system go into a safe state when a failure or abnormality occurs. Examples include railway signals that fall to red or stop when they fail, and normally closed valves that close when power or air pressure is lost.

The design concept of isolating the failed part when part of a system fails and keeping the system as a whole operating, even with reduced function or performance. An example is a system in which several servers share the processing and the rest continue processing when one fails.

The design concept of ensuring that incorrect human operation does not lead to a hazardous state or malfunction, or that incorrect operation is not possible in the first place. Examples include connectors shaped so that they cannot be inserted the wrong way round and equipment that does not start unless its door is closed.

k: フォールトトレランス

n.ja: フォールトトレランス

d: The concept of accepting that parts and equipment will fail and, through means such as redundancy, ensuring that the system as a whole keeps operating correctly even if part of it fails. It is contrasted with fault avoidance, which makes failures themselves less likely.

A technology that combines several disks and uses them like a single storage device to improve speed or reliability. Its levels include RAID 0 (striping, which splits data across disks), RAID 1 (mirroring, which writes the same data to two disks), RAID 5 and RAID 6 (which write parity distributed across the disks), and RAID 10 (which combines mirroring and striping).

A backup method that backs up all data changed since the previous full backup. Each backup grows as the days since the full backup increase, but a restore needs only two: the full backup and the latest differential backup.

A backup method that backs up only the data changed since the previous backup, whether full or incremental. Each backup is small and quick, but a restore requires restoring the full backup and then applying every incremental backup after it in order.

A target expressing to what point in time data must be recoverable when a failure or disaster occurs. With an RPO of 1 hour, at most the last hour of data may be lost, so backups or copies of the data must be taken at least every hour.

A target for the time allowed from the occurrence of a failure or disaster until business operations or the system resume. The shorter the RTO, the more equipment and cost are needed, such as standby systems and backups ready for immediate use.

A digital modulation scheme that represents data by changing both the amplitude and the phase of the carrier. Each symbol sends one of a grid of signal points formed by combinations of in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components, and M-QAM with M points sends log₂ M bits per symbol: 4 bits for 16QAM, 6 for 64QAM and 8 for 256QAM. More levels mean higher speed, but the points are closer together, so a higher S/N is needed.

A scheme that splits data across many mutually orthogonal subcarriers, modulates each at a low symbol rate and sends them in parallel. Setting the subcarrier spacing to the reciprocal of the symbol length lets the subcarriers be separated without interfering even though their spectra overlap. It is robust against multipath and is used in wireless LANs, 4G LTE, 5G NR, digital terrestrial broadcasting and more.

A wireless technique that uses multiple antennas at both the transmitter and the receiver. It raises the transmission rate through spatial multiplexing, sending different data on the same frequency at the same time, or raises reliability through diversity, sending the same data over several paths. The number of streams that spatial multiplexing can send is limited by the smaller of the numbers of transmit and receive antennas.

A technique that adjusts the phase (and amplitude) of each of several antenna elements so that radio waves reinforce one another in a particular direction for transmission or reception. Changing the phases electronically steers the beam without moving the antenna (a phased array). Besides making up for the large propagation loss of millimeter-wave bands, it is used in 5G base stations and wireless LANs to point a beam at each terminal, raising received power and reducing interference.

The rate at which radio power weakens as it spreads out spherically with distance between isotropic antennas in free space with no obstacles or reflections. It is given by L = (4πd/λ)², and in dB it grows by about 6 dB each time the distance doubles and by 20 dB each time it increases tenfold. It is used as the reference propagation loss in link budget calculations.

A calculation that adds up the gains and losses from transmit power to received power to estimate the power reaching the receiver and the margin over the power needed for reception (the sensitivity). It is done in dB and dBm by adding and subtracting terms such as transmit power + antenna gains − propagation loss − cable loss. The same approach is used for power budgets in optical communication as well as radio.

In radio communication, large variation of received power with location, time and frequency. In multipath fading, waves reflected by buildings and other objects arrive over paths of different lengths and interfere, and received power can drop by several tens of dB. The variation becomes faster when the terminal moves. Countermeasures include diversity, OFDM and error-correcting codes.

A problem in wireless LANs that occurs when signals from two terminals both reach the access point but the terminals cannot hear each other because of distance or obstacles. Unaware of each other's transmissions, they transmit at the same time and collide at the access point. It is mitigated by RTS/CTS, in which the CTS returned by the access point makes nearby terminals hold off transmitting.

A theorem stating that for a channel with bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio S/N, the theoretical upper limit on the error-free transmission rate (the channel capacity) is C = B·log₂(1 + S/N). S/N is used as a linear ratio. Capacity is proportional to bandwidth but grows only logarithmically with S/N.

k: スーパーヘテロダイン方式

n.ja: スーパーヘテロダイン方式

d: A receiver architecture that mixes the received signal with the local oscillator (LO) signal in a mixer to convert it to a fixed intermediate frequency (IF) before amplifying and demodulating it. Highly selective filters at the IF remove adjacent channels. Signals at the image frequency, on the opposite side of the LO from the desired signal, are converted to the same IF, so they must be removed before the mixer.

k: ダイレクトコンバージョン方式

n.ja: ダイレクトコンバージョン方式

d: A receiver architecture (zero-IF) that sets the local oscillator (LO) to the received frequency and converts directly to baseband without an intermediate frequency, using two mixers for the in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components. It needs no image-reject or IF filters and is easy to integrate on one CMOS chip. On the other hand, it needs countermeasures against the DC shift (DC offset) caused by LO leakage, 1/f noise and I/Q imbalance.

A measure of how much a circuit such as an amplifier or receiver degrades the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) through its own noise. The input S/N divided by the output S/N (the noise factor), expressed in dB, is called the noise figure (NF). It is defined with thermal noise at 290 K as the reference. The value for cascaded circuits is found with Friis's formula and is set mainly by the first stage's noise figure and gain.

A general term for wireless communication intended to send small amounts of data, such as sensor readings, from devices that run on batteries for years to places several kilometers or more away. Keeping the transmission rate low allows even weak signals to be received, extending the range. Some, such as LoRaWAN, use license-exempt bands (such as the 920 MHz band in Japan), while others, such as LTE-M and NB-IoT, use mobile phone bands.

The variant of the 2.4 GHz short-range wireless technology Bluetooth that emphasizes low power consumption. By keeping communication time very short and shutting down circuits the rest of the time, devices can run a long time even on coin cells. It is used in beacons that periodically send short signals called advertisements, in wearables, sensors and more. It cannot communicate directly with classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR).

Wireless communication over distances of a few centimeters to about 10 cm using electromagnetic induction by a 13.56 MHz magnetic field. The card receives power from the reader's magnetic field, so it needs no battery. It is used in transit IC cards, contactless payments, data exchange between smartphones and more, and FeliCa, widespread in Japan, also uses the same 13.56 MHz.

A machine learning approach that trains a model to predict the correct answer from an input, using data made of pairs of inputs and correct answers (labels). It is called regression when the predicted output is a continuous number and classification when it is one of a fixed set of classes. Models such as linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, support vector machines and neural networks are used. Preparing the labels often takes considerable effort.

A machine learning approach that finds groupings or structure in data that has no correct-answer labels. It is used for clustering, which divides similar data into groups (k-means and others), dimensionality reduction, which represents data with fewer variables (principal component analysis and others), and anomaly detection, which finds data that differs greatly from the rest. No labels need to be prepared, but the quality of the result is harder to evaluate.

A machine learning approach in which an agent (the learner) observes the state of an environment, chooses actions and learns by trial and error a way of choosing actions (a policy) that maximizes the total reward it receives, including future rewards. No correct answer is given for each action, and rewards often arrive with a delay. It is used for games, robot control and for tuning the output of language models to match human evaluations.

A state in which a model memorizes fine details and chance noise in the training data, so that its error on the training data is small but its error on new data (generalization error) is large. It tends to occur when a complex model with many parameters is trained on little data. It is reduced by adding data, simplifying the model, regularization, dropout, early stopping and similar methods.

A method of reducing overfitting by adding to the loss function a penalty term that depends on the size of the weights, keeping the weights from growing too large. L1 regularization, which adds the sum of absolute weight values, tends to drive some weights to exactly zero, while L2 regularization (weight decay), which adds the sum of squared weights, shrinks the weights overall. The penalty strength is a hyperparameter chosen by cross-validation or similar means. In a broader sense, dropout, early stopping and other techniques for improving generalization are also collectively called regularization.

A method that splits the data into k groups, trains on all but one group and evaluates on the remaining one, repeats this k times while rotating the evaluation group, and estimates the model's performance as the average of the k evaluations (k-fold cross-validation). Every data point is used for evaluation exactly once, so limited data is used efficiently and the variation of the estimate caused by how the data happens to be split is reduced. It is used for tuning hyperparameters and selecting models, at roughly k times the computation.

A table that counts the data for each combination of a classification model's prediction and the actual correct answer. For two-class classification it has four cells: true positives (TP), positives correctly predicted as positive; false positives (FP), negatives wrongly predicted as positive; false negatives (FN), positives wrongly predicted as negative; and true negatives (TN), negatives correctly predicted as negative. Accuracy, precision, recall, the F1 score and other metrics can be calculated from it, and it also shows which classes are easily mistaken for which.

n.zh-hant: 精確率與召回率（Precision and recall）

d: Evaluation metrics for two-class classification models. Precision is the fraction of items predicted positive that are actually positive, TP ÷ (TP + FP), and recall is the fraction of actually positive items that were predicted positive, TP ÷ (TP + FN). In general, changing the decision threshold raises one and lowers the other. Their harmonic mean, 2PR ÷ (P + R), is called the F1 score.

An optimization method that computes the gradient of the loss function (the partial derivative with respect to each parameter) and repeatedly moves the parameters a little in the direction opposite to the gradient, searching for parameters that make the loss small. The update is written w ← w − η∇L, where η is called the learning rate. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which uses gradients computed on part of the data (a mini-batch), and its refinements such as momentum and Adam are widely used to train neural networks.

The function applied in each neuron of a neural network to the weighted sum of its inputs (plus a bias). Using a nonlinear function lets a network with stacked layers represent complex relationships. ReLU is common in hidden layers, while output layers often use the sigmoid function for two-class classification, the softmax function for multi-class classification and the identity function (no change) for regression.

k: 畳み込みニューラルネットワーク(CNN)

n.ja: 畳み込みニューラルネットワーク(CNN)

d: A neural network built mainly from convolutional layers, which slide small filters (kernels) over the input and compute sums of products, stacked with pooling layers and others. Because the same filter is reused over the whole input, it has far fewer parameters than fully connected layers and extracts local features such as edges and textures in an image regardless of their position. It is used for image recognition, object detection, audio processing and more.

k: 再帰型ニューラルネットワーク(RNN)

n.ja: 再帰型ニューラルネットワーク(RNN)

d: A neural network that processes sequence data one element at a time and passes the information so far to the next time step as a hidden state. The same weights are reused at every time step, so sequences of different lengths can be handled. Because vanishing gradients readily occur on long sequences, LSTM and GRU, which control the retention and forgetting of information with gates, were devised. Because it must compute in time order and is hard to parallelize, it has been replaced by the Transformer in many language-processing applications.

A method of applying the knowledge (such as ways of extracting features) that a model acquired on one task to a different task. Starting from the weights of a model pretrained on a large amount of data, the output layer is replaced, or part or all of the model is retrained on data for the new task (fine-tuning). It tends to reach high performance with less data and computation than training from scratch, and is widely used in image recognition and language models.

A representative clustering method that divides data into a predetermined number k of clusters. It places k tentative centers, then repeats assigning each data point to the cluster of the nearest center and moving each center to the mean of its cluster's data until the assignments stop changing. It is simple to compute and works on large data, but the result depends on the initial centers, k must be chosen by the user, and clusters that are not roughly spherical are hard to separate.

A dimensionality-reduction method that represents data with many variables using fewer variables while losing as little information as possible. It takes the direction of greatest variance in the data as the first principal component, the direction of greatest variance orthogonal to it as the second, and so on, and represents the data with only the leading components. Mathematically this amounts to finding the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix. It is used for visualizing data, removing noise and preprocessing before training.

A set of books that systematically collects good practice (best practice) for IT service management. Work on it began in a UK government agency, and it has been revised many times and is widely referenced around the world. It describes ideas such as service level management, incident management, problem management, change management, configuration management and the service desk, which organizations adapt to their own needs. It is not a standard; for certification, the international standard for IT service management, ISO/IEC 20000, is used.

The process whose goal is to restore an IT service to normal operation as quickly as possible, using workarounds where needed, when the service stops or degrades because of a failure or similar event (an incident), so that the impact on the business is kept small. It proceeds through logging, categorization and prioritization, investigation and resolution, escalation where needed, and confirmation with the user and closure. Identifying the root cause and preventing recurrence is the role of problem management.

The process whose goal is to identify the root cause (the problem) behind one or more incidents and prevent recurrence with a permanent fix. It includes reactive work, investigating causes from incidents that have occurred, and proactive work, analyzing incident trends to prevent failures that have not happened yet. A problem whose root cause or workaround is known but whose fix is not yet complete is recorded as a known error and shared with the service desk and others. When a fix changes a system, it goes through change management.

The process for preventing failures caused by changes, in which changes to IT services and their components are recorded, assessed for impact, risk and cost, and approved before being carried out. Change requests are received and recorded, and depending on their content they are reviewed at a meeting of the people concerned. An emergency change procedure, in which a small group approves quickly, is also defined for urgent changes. After implementation, the result is checked and the configuration management information is updated.

The process of identifying the components that make up an IT service (configuration items, CIs) and recording their attributes (version, location, owner and so on) and their relationships with other CIs accurately, keeping them up to date. The database that holds these records is called the CMDB (configuration management database). CIs include servers and network equipment, software, documents and the services themselves. Knowing the relationships between CIs makes it easier to determine the scope of a failure and the impact of a change.

A single point of contact (SPOC) that receives all inquiries, failure reports, service requests and the like from users. It records what it receives, resolves what it can itself, escalates what it cannot to specialist technical teams and others, tracks progress and informs users of the outcome. Forms include a local service desk at each site, a centralized one in a single location and a virtual one that links staff in various places over a network.

In IT service management, handing an incident or similar matter that the person in charge cannot resolve alone over to another person or team, or asking someone higher up for a decision. Functional escalation passes it to a technical team with the specialist knowledge or authority needed to resolve it, while hierarchical escalation reports to higher management to obtain decisions or resources when the target time is about to be exceeded or the impact is large. The conditions for escalation and the contacts are decided in advance.

The average time it takes to repair a failed system or device and return it to a usable state (Mean Time To Repair). It includes the time to detect the failure, isolate the cause, replace parts or fix the settings, and verify the result. Availability is expressed as MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR), so the shorter the MTTR, the higher the availability. It is shortened by monitoring that detects failures quickly, spare parts on hand, well-prepared procedures and automatic failover.

A plan prepared in advance so that critical business activities are not interrupted, or are resumed within an acceptable time if they are, even when natural disasters, large-scale failures, epidemics and the like occur (Business Continuity Plan). A business impact analysis determines the critical activities and the acceptable downtime, and the plan sets out alternative sites and staff, procedures for recovering systems and so on. The whole ongoing effort of drawing up, exercising and reviewing the plan is called business continuity management (BCM).

An activity in which specialist auditors independent of the audited area (systems auditors) inspect and evaluate whether controls over the risks associated with information systems are properly designed and operated, and report the results to management and others as assurance or as advice for improvement. It proceeds through audit planning, a preliminary survey, the main audit, evaluation and conclusion, audit reporting and follow-up. In Japan, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry publishes the System Audit Standards and the System Management Standards.

Records that make it possible to trace and verify afterward the flow of a transaction or data from input through processing, output and storage, and who did what and when. Access and operation logs, processing records and approval records are examples. Auditors follow them to verify that processing was legitimate and accurate. Mechanisms that protect them from tampering or deletion and keep them for the required period are considered from the system design stage.

The mechanisms and procedures built into an organization's operations and carried out by everyone in it in order to achieve the organization's objectives. In the framework of Japan's internal control reporting system (J-SOX), the objectives are effectiveness and efficiency of operations, reliability of reporting, compliance with laws and regulations related to business activities, and safeguarding of assets, and the basic components are the control environment, risk evaluation and response, control activities, information and communication, monitoring, and response to IT. It is based on the U.S. COSO framework.

The system by which management (the board and senior executives) takes responsibility for directing IT investment and use, evaluating its execution and results and monitoring it, so that the use of IT supports the organization's goals and strategy. The international standard ISO/IEC 38500 describes the role of the governing body as Evaluate, Direct and Monitor. Day-to-day operations management and the management of individual projects are management activities carried out under that direction.

An internal control principle that divides responsibilities and authority so that no single person can complete, alone, the initiation (input), approval, recording and custody of assets for a transaction. Errors and fraud cannot be completed by one person's decision, and they are easier to find through mutual checks. In information systems, it is applied by separating the people who develop programs from those who deploy them to production and operate them, and by separating the authority to enter data from the authority to approve it.

k: CAAT(コンピュータ支援監査技法)

n.ja: CAAT(コンピュータ支援監査技法)

d: A collective term for techniques that use computers to perform audit procedures (Computer Assisted Audit Techniques). They include the test data method, in which a program processes data prepared by the auditor and the results are checked; the ITF method, which sets up fictitious audit accounts in the production system; the snapshot method, which writes out data midway through processing; parallel simulation, in which the auditor's own program processes production data and the results are compared; and extraction and analysis of data with generalized audit software. They allow large volumes of data to be examined in full.

Ways of counting the number of cases when some items are chosen from a set. A permutation distinguishes the order of the chosen items: the number of ways to choose and arrange r of n items is nPr = n!/(n − r)!. A combination ignores the order: nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!) = nPr/r!. With repetition allowed, there are nʳ arrangements. They are the basis of probability calculations and are also used to estimate the total number of PINs or the number of test combinations.

The probability that event A occurs given that event B has occurred. It is written P(A | B) and calculated as P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). It amounts to treating only the cases in which B occurred as the whole and considering the fraction of them in which A occurs. P(A | B) and P(B | A) are generally different values, and Bayes' theorem links the two. If A and B are independent, P(A | B) = P(A).

The relation that reverses the direction of a conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) ÷ P(B). It is used to update the prior probability P(A) of a cause A into the posterior probability P(A | B) on the basis of an observed result B. It is used for calculating the positive predictive value of a test, for spam filtering (naive Bayes) and for estimating the causes of failures. It also shows the effect of the base rate: when the cause is rare, many positives are false even for an accurate test.

The average value taken by a quantity determined by chance. It is found by multiplying each possible value by the probability of that value and adding the results. For example, the expected value of a die roll is (1 + 2 + … + 6) ÷ 6 = 3.5. The expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values (linearity of expectation), and this holds even for quantities that are not independent. It is used for comparing countermeasures by expected loss, for decision making and for calculating averages in queueing.

A quantity expressing the size of the spread of data or of a random variable, often written σ (sigma). The variance is the average of the squared differences between each value and the mean, and the standard deviation is its positive square root. It has the same unit as the original data, so the width of the spread can be expressed directly, as in the mean ±1σ or ±3σ. It is widely used for control limits in process control, process capability indices, evaluating measurement errors and calculations with the normal distribution.

The probability distribution of the number of successes when a trial with success probability p is repeated n times independently. The probability of exactly k successes is nCk × pᵏ × (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, the mean is np and the variance is np(1 − p). For example, when 10 parts are taken from a population with a 10% defect rate, the probability that none is defective is 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.349. It is used to calculate the acceptance probability of sampling inspection and the number of bit errors in communication, and when n is large and p is small it can be approximated by a Poisson distribution.

The probability distribution of the number of times a rare event that occurs independently happens within a fixed time or area. With mean λ, the probability of k occurrences is λᵏ × e^(−λ) ÷ k!, and both the mean and the variance are λ. It is used to model the number of requests arriving at a server, the number of inquiries to a service desk, the number of defects on a wafer and the number of photons. The probability of zero defects, e^(−λ), corresponds to the Poisson yield model. When the number of arrivals follows a Poisson distribution, the intervals between arrivals follow an exponential distribution.

A continuous probability distribution with a symmetric bell shape centered on the mean μ, whose shape is determined by the mean μ and the standard deviation σ. It is also called the Gaussian distribution. About 68% lies within the mean ±1σ, about 95% within ±2σ and about 99.7% within ±3σ. A quantity formed by adding many small independent factors approaches a normal distribution (the central limit theorem), so it is widely used as a model of measurement errors and manufacturing variation. Standardizing with z = (x − μ) ÷ σ gives the standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

A continuous probability distribution followed by the intervals between randomly occurring events and by the time to failure of a part with a constant failure rate. With rate λ, the probability that the event does not occur by time t is e^(−λt), and the mean is 1/λ. It is memoryless: the distribution of the remaining time does not depend on how much time has already passed. It is used as the model of the intervals between arrivals when the number of arrivals follows a Poisson distribution and of the time to failure in the random-failure period, and it is an assumption of the M/M/1 queueing model.

The value in the middle when data are sorted by size. When there is an even number of values, it is the average of the two middle values. Unlike the mean, it is little affected by values far from the rest (outliers), so it suits as the representative value of data that include some extreme values, such as response times or incomes. Half of the data are at or below it and half at or above it, and it corresponds to the second quartile. The most frequent value is called the mode.

The values at the positions that divide data sorted by size into four equal parts, called from the smallest the first quartile, the second quartile (the median) and the third quartile. The interquartile range, the third quartile minus the first, is the width containing the middle half of the data and is a measure of spread little affected by outliers. A box plot shows the quartiles as a box and the minimum, maximum and so on as whiskers, making the shapes of distributions easy to compare. There are several conventions for computing quartiles, and the values differ slightly between methods.

A measure expressing the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two quantities as a value from −1 to 1. It is calculated by dividing the covariance of x and y by the product of the standard deviation of x and the standard deviation of y. The closer it is to 1, the stronger the positive correlation; the closer to −1, the stronger the negative correlation; close to 0, the linear relationship is weak. Curved relationships hardly show up in the correlation coefficient, and correlation does not mean that one quantity causes the other. The slope of the regression line is the correlation coefficient multiplied by the ratio of the standard deviations of the two quantities.

An interval that estimates an unknown value, such as the population mean, from a sample with a range. A 95% confidence interval is made by a method such that, if sampling were repeated, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true value. When the population standard deviation σ is known, the 95% confidence interval for the population mean is the sample mean ± 1.96 × σ/√n, where σ/√n is called the standard error. Making the sample size n four times as large halves the width of the interval.

A statistical method for judging, on the basis of data, whether to reject a hypothesis such as "there is no difference". The hypothesis to be refuted is set up as the null hypothesis, and the probability of obtaining a result equal to or more extreme than the one observed, assuming it is true (the p-value), is calculated. If the p-value is smaller than a significance level decided in advance (such as 5%), the null hypothesis is rejected. There are type I errors, rejecting a true null hypothesis, and type II errors, failing to reject a false one.

The theory that models with probability how processing requests arrive at a window or server and wait until it is free to be served, and that derives waiting times and queue lengths. A model is described in Kendall's notation, which lists the arrival distribution, service time distribution and number of servers, as in "M/M/1". In the M/M/1 model, the average waiting time is ρ/(1 − ρ) × Ts, using the utilization ρ = arrival rate λ × average service time Ts. It is used in computer performance evaluation, network delay analysis and analysis of work in progress in factories.

The application-layer protocol for exchanging HTML, images and data between web browsers and web servers, among others. A client sends a request made up of a method, a URL, headers and a body, and the server returns a response made up of a status code, headers and a body. As a protocol it is stateless, so state such as a login is kept with cookies and similar means. HTTP/1.1 uses a text format and persistent connections, HTTP/2 multiplexes several streams over one TCP connection, and HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP. HTTP protected by TLS is called HTTPS.

A three-digit number in the first line of an HTTP response that indicates the result of the request.
