Examples include operating-system APIs, library APIs and web APIs that exchange data over HTTP, such as REST APIs. Callers do not need to know the implementation, and the implementation can be replaced as long as the API stays the same. The equivalent agreement at the machine-code level is called the ABI.

The common name for wireless LANs based on the IEEE 802.11 standards; the name shows that a device is certified by the industry group Wi-Fi Alliance. It mainly uses the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands and connects devices to a LAN through access points. Access to the air is coordinated with CSMA/CA, and speed and efficiency come from OFDM, MIMO and, from Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax), OFDMA. Traffic is encrypted with WPA2 or WPA3.

k: ルーティング(経路制御)

n.ja: ルーティング(経路制御)

d: Deciding which path packets take to reach their destination on an IP network. Each router holds a routing table, picks the route that matches the destination IP address with the longest prefix (longest-prefix match) and passes the packet to the next router. The table is built by static routing, configured by hand, or by dynamic routing, built automatically with routing protocols such as OSPF, RIP and BGP.

The largest packet a link can carry in one piece; 1500 bytes is standard for Ethernet. An IP packet larger than this is fragmented along the way or dropped in IPv4, while in IPv6 only the source fragments. The mechanism for finding the smallest MTU along a path is called path MTU discovery. When extra headers are added, as in VPN tunnels, the space left for the payload shrinks accordingly.

An error-control method in which the receiver, on finding errors or missing data, gets correct data by having the sender send it again. The receiver returns acknowledgments (ACKs) or negative acknowledgments (NAKs), and the sender retransmits if no ACK arrives within a set time. Variants include stop-and-wait, which confirms one unit at a time, Go-Back-N and selective repeat. It is used in TCP, wireless LANs and the data link layer of PCI Express, among others, and is often combined with forward error correction (FEC).

HTTP protected by TLS. It encrypts exchanges, detects tampering and authenticates the server with a server certificate. URLs start with https:// and the default port number is 443. Requests and responses have the same form as in HTTP, with a TLS layer underneath.

A mechanism that builds an encrypted virtual private channel (a tunnel) over a shared network such as the internet, so that distant sites and outside devices communicate as if they were connected directly to the internal network. Methods include IPsec, TLS (SSL-VPN) and WireGuard.

A transport-layer protocol that runs over UDP. It builds in TLS 1.3 encryption and combines connection setup and key exchange into one round trip. It multiplexes several streams in one connection, and losing a packet on one stream does not stall the others. It is the basis of HTTP/3 and was standardized by the IETF as RFC 9000 in 2021.

A mechanism (a device or software), usually placed at a network boundary, that passes only traffic allowed by predefined rules and blocks everything else. It decides by source and destination IP addresses, port numbers, protocol, direction of traffic and so on. Its main job is to protect an internal network from unauthorized connections from the internet.

The input–output relation of a linear time-invariant system expressed as the ratio G(s) = Y(s)/X(s) of the Laplace transforms of output and input with all initial values zero. It equals the Laplace transform of the impulse response. Values of s that make the denominator zero are poles and those that make the numerator zero are zeros; the pole positions show stability and speed of response. Setting s = jω gives the frequency response. For discrete-time systems it is written H(z) using the z-transform.

A method that transforms a function of time f(t) (t ≥ 0) into a function of the complex variable s, F(s) = ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^(−st) dt. With zero initial values, differentiation corresponds to multiplying by s and integration to dividing by s, so linear differential equations can be handled as algebraic expressions in s. It is the basic tool for finding transfer functions in control engineering, and for discrete-time systems the z-transform plays the same role. A unit step transforms to 1/s and e^(−at) to 1/(s + a).

A diagram of a control system that shows each element as a box (block) containing its transfer function, the flow of signals as arrows, the addition and subtraction of signals as summing points and the branching of signals as pickoff points. Blocks in series combine into the product of their transfer functions and blocks in parallel into the sum, and a negative-feedback loop can be replaced by a single block G/(1 + GH). Repeating such equivalent transformations gives the transfer function from the setpoint or a disturbance to the output.

A system whose transfer function is G(s) = K/(1 + Ts), where K is the steady-state gain and T the time constant. Its output for a step input is K(1 − e^(−t/T)), reaching about 63.2% of the final value at t = T, about 95% at 3T and about 99.3% at 5T, with no overshoot. Many familiar systems, such as RC circuits, thermal systems and liquid-level systems, can be approximated in this form. In the frequency response, the gain falls at −20 dB/dec above the corner angular frequency 1/T.

A system whose transfer function is G(s) = Kωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²), where ωn is the natural angular frequency and ζ the damping ratio. For 0 < ζ < 1 the step response approaches the final value while oscillating, for ζ = 1 it settles fastest without overshoot and for ζ > 1 it approaches slowly. Mechanical spring–mass–damper systems, RLC circuits and position control loops take this form. Higher-order systems are also often approximated by their two dominant poles.

The output going past its final value in a step response or similar, and also the maximum amount by which it does so. In control engineering it is expressed as a percentage of the final value; for a second-order system without zeros it is exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)), determined by the damping ratio ζ alone. In feedback control systems, the smaller the phase margin, the larger the overshoot. In electronic circuits, the same word is used when a signal or voltage waveform temporarily exceeds its final level because of wiring inductance or reflections.

The time from applying a step input until the output enters a specified band around its final value (such as ±2% or ±5%) and stays within it. It describes the speed and the settling of a response together; for a second-order system the ±2% settling time is estimated at about 4/(ζωn) and the ±5% one at about 3/(ζωn). The ±2% settling time of a first-order system is about 3.9T, where T is the time constant. In specifications for A/D converters and op-amps, the time for the output to settle to a specified accuracy is also called the settling time.

The difference between the setpoint and the controlled variable that remains after the response of a control system has settled; it is also called offset. In a unity-feedback system it is 1/(1 + Kp) for a step setpoint, where Kp = G(0) is the position error constant, and it does not become zero in a system with no integrator in the forward path (type 0). In a type 1 system, with one integrator, the steady-state error to a step is zero, and an error of 1/Kv (Kv is the velocity error constant) remains for a ramp setpoint. The integral action of PI control is used to remove this error.

k: ラウス・フルビッツの安定判別法

n.ja: ラウス・フルビッツの安定判別法

d: A method that decides, from the coefficients of the characteristic equation alone and without solving it, whether all its roots (the closed-loop poles) lie in the left half of the s-plane. A necessary condition is that all coefficients have the same sign with no missing term; in addition, the system is stable if the first column of the Routh array all has the same sign, and the number of sign changes equals the number of roots in the right half-plane. A cubic s³ + a₂s² + a₁s + a₀ = 0 is stable when all coefficients are positive and a₂a₁ > a₀. It is used to find the range of a gain for which a system is stable. Routh's method and Hurwitz's method give the same conditions.

A representation of the frequency response of a system as two graphs with the logarithm of frequency on the horizontal axis and the gain (dB) and phase (degrees) on the vertical axes. A product of transfer functions becomes a sum of gains (in dB) and phases, so the plot can be drawn by adding up the lines of each element. Each additional pole changes the gain slope by −20 dB/dec and adds up to 90° of phase lag. The gain margin and phase margin are read from the Bode plot of the loop transfer function to examine stability.

The amount, in decibels, by which the gain of the loop transfer function is below 0 dB at the frequency where its phase reaches −180° (the phase crossover frequency). It shows by what factor the loop gain could be raised before the loop becomes unstable; for example, with a gain margin of about 9.5 dB, tripling the gain reaches the stability limit. Together with the phase margin it expresses the stability margin, and about 10 to 20 dB is a common guideline for servo systems.

Feedback control that sets the manipulated variable by adding a term proportional to the error e (P), a term proportional to the integral of the error (I) and a term proportional to the derivative of the error (D). It is written u = Kp(e + (1/Ti)∫e dt + Td·de/dt), where Kp is the proportional gain, Ti the integral time and Td the derivative time. The proportional term provides speed, the integral term removes the steady-state error and the derivative term suppresses oscillation. Its structure is simple, and it is used in most industrial control loops, for temperature, motors, power supplies, chemical processes and more.

A phenomenon in which the integral term of a PID controller keeps accumulating the error and grows excessively while the manipulated variable is saturated at an upper or lower limit of the actuator. Even after the error changes sign, the manipulated variable stays saturated until the accumulated integral comes down, causing a large overshoot and a long oscillation. It is prevented by anti-windup measures such as conditional integration (clamping), which stops integrating during saturation, back-calculation, which feeds the difference between the values before and after limiting back into the integrator, and the use of the velocity form of PID.

k: フィードフォワード制御

n.ja: フィードフォワード制御

d: Control that measures disturbances or setpoint changes and, before they affect the controlled variable, applies a manipulated variable calculated from a model of the plant. It does not wait for an error to appear, so it responds quickly, but it cannot correct model errors or unmeasured disturbances, so it is usually combined with feedback control. Its path lies outside the loop, so it does not change the stability of the feedback loop. In semiconductor fabs, adjusting the conditions of a process step based on measurements from an earlier step is also called feedforward control.

Control that measures the controlled variable with a sensor, compares it with the setpoint and changes the manipulated variable to reduce the difference (the error). Because the signal goes around a loop, it is also called closed-loop control. It corrects deviations in the result whatever their cause, so it is robust to disturbances and plant changes, but it corrects only after an error appears, so there is a delay, and too high a gain leads to oscillation or instability. PID control is the typical example, widely used to control temperature, speed, voltage, position and more.
